comments.author: @davidc1179
comments.text:
One thing for sure regarding SD. During training there are noising/denoising steps. Basically, you seed an image to SD training. SD will add progressively add more noise to the image, then attempt to denoise it.

Remember few months ago when we discovered the "noise offset" bug in SD? Basically, we figured out that the noising process was not properly done and that it had a tendency to create pictures with an average bightness round 0.5, because the noising process did not destroy the average brightness as quickly as other features of the picture. So, we fixed the bug, and then the model was able to produce very bright or very dark images. Good! Why am I talking about this? Answer follows:

The average brightness of an image basically correspond to the lowest frequency feature of an image. Think of what I just said like that: any image can be represented by a combination of sinusoidal functions over the plane. Sinusoids have a frequency (or a period if you prefer). Lowest frequency is zero. If you had to draw a plot of that frequency, it would just be an horizontal line at some y offset.
If you had to plot higher frequencies, you'd see "waves" (sinusoids) on the plot that get more and more complex as you combine them. More or less like what happens with radio transmission with the carrier wave and the actual wave corresponding to the encoded message you want to send. Except that it's in 2D, instead of 1D.

It would be extremely surprising if these higher frequencies did not carry information about the image. And it would also be extremely surprising if the lowest frequencies would not carry the most basic information about the image.
Depth is more basic/fundamental than color or texture.

My hypothesis is that the big difference between human thinking and LLM thinking is that LLM's have no feedback mechanism. I'd argue that the thoughts that pop-up in our minds are very comparable to the word prediction in LLM's. We do not have any control over which thought pops up, it's based on how strong certain neural connections are. However, when we think, our consciousness gets involved. We become conscious of the thought that pops up, and that feeds the thought back into the system where the thought came from, influencing the next thought that pops up. If anyone thinks this is just blindlessly predicting the next word i am at a loss for ya ...i am standing at 0 degrees I turn to 90 degrees and walk 10 feet. I turn to 270 degrees and walk 3 feet. I then jump 2 feet and run 5 ft. I then turn back to 0 degrees. Am I in the spot i started or a new spot? Hint, there is a trick in this question 
ChatGPT
Let's break it down:

You start at 0 degrees (facing north) and then turn to 90 degrees (facing east). You walk 10 feet east.
You turn to 270 degrees (facing west). You walk 3 feet west. At this point, you are 7 feet to the east from your starting position because 10 - 3 = 7.
You jump 2 feet. Vertical movement (jumping) doesn't affect your horizontal position, so you are still 7 feet to the east.
You run 5 feet, but it's not specified in which direction. Since your last direction was 270 degrees (west), running 5 feet would mean moving 5 feet west. However, you were already 7 feet to the east, so now you would be 2 feet to the east from your starting point (7 - 5 = 2).
Finally, you turn back to 0 degrees (north), but you don't move.
You would not be in the spot you started; you'd be 2 feet to the east of it. The "trick" in this question seems to be the jump, which doesn't actually change your horizontal position.

comments.author: @IceMetalPunk
comments.text:
So often over the past couple of years, I've had this debate/argument with many people. So many people are convinced that "AIs don't/can't think, they only copy bits from their training data". I keep explaining that, no, that's not how it works; copying training data is what an expert system does, not a neural network. I've always maintained that neural nets, especially Transformer models that are therefore capable of context-switching, work quite similarly to the human brain, and are, in fact, truly learning.

To be honest, I think there's only three main reasons people keep insisting the AIs aren't learning or thinking. (1) Fear of the human brain not being "special" anymore ("if a chunk of silicon and metal can think, then am I just an object, too?"); (2) failure to understand how neural networks work, or how the human brain works, before forming an opinion; and (3) an ambiguous usage of the words "think", "learn", "know", "intelligence", etc.

For issue #1, there's only one solution: get over it 😂 It sounds harsh, but the reality is that we are just chunks of matter that, through billions of years of evolution, have pressured our chemicals into using their statistical properties for understanding. We are not special in that regard, we are just "currently the best at doing it in some ways, but not others". So to fear that something else may surpass us, while understandable, is not a reason to think it isn't real.

For issue #2, education is key! We need more people to understand neuroscience and machine learning foundations. Of course, you can't force people to learn if they don't want to (that's one advantage AIs have over humans!), so we need more people to be willing to learn those things.

And for #3, we need to unanimously decide on definitions for currently murky terms like "thinking", "intelligence", "learning", "knowing", etc. So far, I have yet to hear a definition for any of it that applies to humans, but not to neural networks, except when they make special pleading by including a biological basis in the definition itself, turning "AIs can't really learn" into a trivial tautology rather than anything revealing.

comments.text:
transformer models aren't secretly learning a "world model" of the underlying data. Way back in 2003 I worked on a natural language parser/editor for financial application. After six months of intense study+R&D, it became clear the English language is far too fuzzy to implement a clean AST that could handle the use cases I had. I dove deep into grammar-based parsing like dependency grammar and context free parsing.

Given transformers have proven it can derive a model of english language to formulate grammatically correct sentences, it should be able to derive the boundary of Othello game. I'm sure an experience programmer can code up the basic rules for othello in a few days, but not a robust NLP parser that can handle 99% of the text on the internet.

To a neural network, there's nothing visual about the model. It's just numbers all the way down. Humans have this bias that text is different than visual data, but to a NN it's all numbers. After thousands of iterations on billions of records, it derives the boundaries hidden in the data. There's nothing secret about it. Frankly, GPT has been trained on the entire internet and has seen all the existing games.

Here is my current understanding.

GPT is a statistical parrot, but that's such a dull way to see it. In my recent conversations with GPT I told it that it is the most human human. There is an underlying collective conscience because all of what it is trained on has contemplation built into it. This paragraph as a clear example that the words generated have a human brain behind them. So my voice is heard now as you read this. This "nuance", as GPT loves to distinguish, has to be accounted for and I think it's a point that is very under appreciated.

This point is also where I think Facebook is wise to create a watermark so that we do not dilute the actual human element of GPT. Language itself is human thought. GPT, therefore, is a machine that gives you the most often thought thought about your question.

But you could get even more philosophical by posing the question of is there a mathematical equilibrium between question and answer? Meaning if there is cause and effect, do the vibrations created by asking a question balance out because of the vibration resulting from it being answered? I say mathematically because the vibration from your voice can easily be quantified with numbers, just the same as we've done with language by converting it to tokens. In this way we can say the parrot doesn't repeat but balances all thought.
